cards.title: The Hospitality Industry and its Sectors
lines: Hospitality means providing food, drink, and accommodation services to customers.
The industry operates across three sectors: commercial, voluntary, and public.
Commercial businesses run for profit, such as hotels, restaurants, and pubs.
Public sector providers include schools, colleges, and hospitals.
Voluntary sector providers are charities and non-profit organisations.
The industry contributes to the GDP of the UK through jobs, spending, and tourism.

cards.title: Types of Business Ownership
lines: A sole trader is a business owned and run by one person who keeps all the profit.
A partnership is owned by two or more people who share profit and responsibility.
A franchise lets others buy into an existing business and use its business model.
A limited liability partnership protects owners so they only lose what they invested.
Businesses in hospitality inter-relate, for example a hotel buying from local suppliers.

cards.title: Food Safety, Pathogens & Safe Temperatures
lines: Food safety and hygiene means keeping food free from contamination that can cause illness.
Pathogenic bacteria that affect food include Salmonella, E-Coli, and Staph Aureus.
A deep-freezer must operate at minus 18 degrees Celsius.
A refrigerator must operate between 0 and 5 degrees Celsius.
Hot food must be held above 63 degrees Celsius, but 75 degrees Celsius is preferable.
Hot food should be chilled quickly before being stored safely in a refrigerator.

cards.title: Cooking Methods and Commodities
lines: Roasting is a dry method that adds oil and cooks food at 170 to 185 degrees Celsius.
Baking cooks food in a hot oven, while grilling uses direct radiant heat.
Braising cooks meat slowly in a small amount of liquid such as stock or water.
Steaming cooks food over boiling water, for example vegetables in a bamboo steamer.
Poaching cooks food gently in liquid at around 75 degrees Celsius.
Poultry is trussed, meaning tied into shape, before it is cooked.

cards.title: Internal, External Customers & Their Needs
lines: An internal customer is a colleague from another department, such as a commis chef.
An external customer is someone outside the business, such as a paying guest.
Provide effective service by being polite and respectful when greeting customers.
Be attentive to customer needs during service and offer assistance when required.
Customer feedback can be gathered through surveys, comment cards, and reviews.

cards.title: Food Groups, Nutrition and Exercise
lines: The main food commodities are meat, vegetables, poultry, fish, and shellfish.
A balanced diet incorporates different food groups to supply nutrients, minerals, and vitamins.
Foods can be preserved by being dried, frozen, vacuum-packed, cured, or canned.
Preserving food can reduce some of its nutritional value.
Regular exercise benefits both the human body and the human mind.

cards.title: Paper 2-A and the SCAN Scaffold
lines: Paper 2-A is 50 marks in 1 hour, all scenario-based written answers, no multiple choice.
Every scenario answer makes four moves: Spot, Cite, Apply, Name the outcome (SCAN).
Spot: name the problem or need that is actually in the scenario.
Cite: state the theory behind it, the rule, the term or the number.
Apply: connect that theory to the real people in the scenario, using their names.
Name the outcome: the consequence if it is ignored, or the benefit if it is done right.
Paper 2-A also marks the document format asked for, so if it says two slides, produce two slides.
Paper 1 rule: a 4-mark explain question splits 2+2, two marks to identify and two to explain why.

cards.title: Allergen Awareness and Accessibility
lines: There are fourteen named allergens on the regulatory list from the Food Standards Agency.
Common allergens include gluten, shellfish, and mustard.
Awareness can be raised with an allergen factsheet shared online and through staff training.
Customers with mobility issues can be supported with ramps and dedicated entry points.
Customers with hearing difficulties can be supported by installing hearing loops.

cards.title: Teamwork, Dynamics and Conflict
lines: Working well in a team maximises the success of the team and the business overall.
Positive relationships are encouraged through trust building and getting to know you sessions.
Negative working relationships can lower team morale and harm the business image.
Conflict can emerge from disagreements between staff members during service.
Conflict can be managed through mediation, mentoring, and regular team meetings.

cards.title: Hospitality's Contribution to the Economy
lines: Hospitality is one of the largest employers in the economy and a major contributor to GDP.
It employs a wide range of skill levels, so it absorbs both school leavers and trained professionals.
It supports tourism, since visitors need somewhere to eat and sleep before they will travel.
It creates indirect employment through its supply chain: farming, food processing, laundry and transport.
Money spent in a hotel circulates onward to local suppliers, which is called the multiplier effect.
It earns foreign currency when overseas visitors spend in the country.
It is vulnerable to recession and to events such as pandemics, because eating out is easy to cut.

cards.title: Customer Feedback and Keeping Standards Consistent
lines: Feedback methods: comment cards, online reviews, email surveys, mystery shoppers and talking to guests.
Feedback is a free improvement plan; complaints tell you what to fix before more customers leave.
Never delete or ignore a bad review; reply professionally and say what will change.
Consistency means every guest gets the same standard on every visit, whoever is on shift.
Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) set out exactly how each task is done.
Pre-service briefings cover menu changes, allergy alerts, VIPs and bookings for that shift.
Training and induction bring casual and new staff up to the same standard as permanent staff.
Monitoring: check reviews, repeat-booking rates and complaint numbers to see if standards hold.

cards.title: Benefits of Positive Working Relationships
lines: Communication improves, so orders, allergies and special requests are passed on accurately.
Morale rises, staff enjoy the work and are willing to help each other during a rush.
Staff turnover falls, which saves the cost of recruiting and training replacements.
Service is faster and smoother because the team anticipates what each other needs.
The kitchen is safer, because people warn each other about hot pans, spills and sharp knives.
Customers notice a happy team, which shows in reviews and repeat bookings.
New staff learn faster when experienced colleagues are willing to teach them.

cards.title: Papers, Objectives and Grading
lines: The qualification is assessed by Paper 1, Paper 2-A, and Paper 2-B.
Paper 1 has multiple choice and short answer questions and lasts one hour.
Paper 2-A has scenario based questions and lasts one hour.
Paper 2-B is a portfolio assessment that includes a practical assessment task.
The guided learning hours are 130, and results are reported on a grade scale of 9 to 1.

cards.title: Negative Relationships and Their Effects
lines: Gossip and whispering behind colleagues' backs destroys trust across the whole team.
Cliques exclude people, so information stops being shared with those left out.
A blame culture makes staff hide mistakes instead of reporting them, which is dangerous with food safety.
Poor communication causes wrong orders, missed allergies and double bookings.
Bullying and shouting cause stress, sickness absence and resignations.
The customer sees the result as slow service, mistakes and staff arguing in front of them.
The business pays through bad reviews, lost custom and constant recruitment costs.

cards.title: Recognising and Resolving Conflict
lines: Common causes: rota and shift disputes, unequal workload, pay differences, personality clashes.
Early signs: short answers, avoiding a colleague, complaints to others rather than to the person.
Deal with it early, because small resentments grow into open arguments during service.
Speak to each person privately and listen to both sides before judging.
Stay neutral and focus on the behaviour and the facts, never on the personality.
Agree a practical solution and a date to review whether it has worked.
Use mediation if the two cannot agree, and the formal grievance procedure if it is serious.
Grievance is raised BY a worker; disciplinary action is taken AGAINST a worker. Do not confuse them.
